#899. Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

Manuel Neuer's latest injury gives Jonas Urbig a run of games in Bayern's goal. Marc-André ter Stegen remains Germany’s No. 1, but Urbig now has a chance to strengthen his case for the future.

It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

#897. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

It is all change at Villa and, although a little trepidation is inevitable, a refresh was probably overdue. At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. #895. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

#893. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#892. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

#890. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

#889. Jennifer Lawrence Reacts to Connor Wood Comment Going Viral

After Jennifer Lawrence playfully called out DWTS season 35 contestant Connor Wood for paying her “no mind,” despite naming her as his celebrity crush, she reacted to the quip going viral.

Jennifer Lawrence was paying no mind to what the internet would think of this quip.

After The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping actress playfully called out Connor Wood for ignoring her when they once crossed paths, she admitted she didn’t think it would get so much attention.

“I don’t really know how to feel about it,” Lawrence told Andy Cohen during a Nov. 19 appearance on Watch What Happens Live alongside costar Josh Hutcherson. “I did not expect that to go viral. I don’t really get it.”

Lawrence—who joined Instagram in September—dropped the now-viral comment last month on a clip of Wood sharing she was his celebrity crush, and he wanted her to notice him.

“I just want a little acknowledgment from Jennifer Lawrence that I’m funny,” he said in an Oct. 20 Instagram video. “And that’s all I need.”

He joked, “Jennifer, I really need something good to happen to me.”

To which Lawrence revealed he’d already had his chance in a comment that now has over 100,000 likes, “I saw you on 8th avenue drinking a smoothie and you paid me no mind.”

Wood later reacted to the comment in a video shared by his Dancing With the Stars season 35 dance partner Rylee Arnold.

“‘I saw you on Eighth Avenue drinking a smoothie and you paid me no mind,’” Wood read over and over in the video. “It’s rolling around in my head.”

As Wood neared tears in the video, Arnold assured, “Don’t be upset! She’s doing that to be funny.”

Later, the 31-year-old embraced the comment, stepping out in a T-shirt with the quote emblazoned on the front, as well as striking up a brand deal with Smoothie King.

While the moment has inspired memes and even merchandise, it didn’t go viral for everyone. As Hutcherson joked during WWHL of the ordeal, “I don’t know what any of those words mean.”

Lawrence, meanwhile, had one correction to make. It wasn’t Eighth Avenue after all. As she noted, “It was also Greenwich.”

To pay some mind to more of the DWTS season 35 contestants ahead of the finale, keep reading…

#887. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust. Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met. Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. In 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. The exhibition opens amid renewed debates over settler colonialism, the definition of genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over German support for Israel during the war in Gaza. These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance.  However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy. "I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

#885. Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’

A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty

In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

Scared, exhausted and running on adrenaline, the team had lived through another episode of disruption; but in truth they had rarely known stability. For Syrian women’s footballers, navigating uncertainty had been part of the game long before the country’s political upheaval reached its latest turning point. “My generation was burned away and completely lost,” said Noor Jumaa, a former national team goalkeeper. “It was like everything that was being built just disappeared.”

After 14 years of war, Syria has much to rebuild. Women’s football is among the institutions trying to recover from a conflict that erased an entire generation of players, interrupted the development of the game itself and left its infrastructure struggling. Yet, in recent years, Syria’s youth teams have emerged as one of the country’s more unexpected sporting success stories, winning regional titles and producing players who are beginning to make their mark abroad.

Syria’s women’s national team played their first international match in 2005. By 2011, plans were under way for an 11-a-side women’s league. Then the uprising began, and all plans were abandoned. For the next six years, women’s football in Syria effectively stopped. There were no international fixtures at any level, only occasional futsal tournaments. More than six million people eventually fled Syria, including hundreds involved in the sport, leaving an already small pool of players scattered across the world.

Men’s football, by contrast, continued. The national team played matches abroad after Syria was barred from hosting fixtures in 2011 on security grounds. The Assad regime used its successes to project an image of normality, even welcoming the squad to his palace after their 2012 WAFF Championship victory. Fifa, despite its rules against political interference, stayed silent.

Girls growing up in those years had no women’s team to watch. “I was watching a match of Syria’s men’s national team, and I was really upset. I would say, ‘God, if only they’d make a national team for girls,’” recalled Raneem Abo Lateef, a 21-year-old goalkeeper for Syria. The opportunity came unexpectedly after her family moved houses, and a girl next door told Abo Lateef that a relative was starting a girls’ club. “Girls’ football? Wow,” she said. “It was like dreams coming true.”

Similarly, international teammate Julnar Mustafa spent hours playing with boys in her neighbourhood in Hasakah. Born in 2008, so too young to remember the beginning of the uprising, she filmed herself dribbling and performing tricks on her phone, uploading the videos to Facebook. A regional coach came across them and invited Mustafa to join his team.

But finding an opportunity to play was only part of the challenge. “In our society, especially in the north, in Hasakah, sport is completely off-limits for girls,” Mustafa told the Guardian. “Not football, not anything”.

While a new generation of girls were finding their way into football, the national team was attempting to return to international competition. In April 2017, Syria entered the Asian Cup qualifiers in Vietnam, assembling a squad after six years without any activity. The federation announced tryouts on Facebook, and players were given about a month of preparation. Syria went on to lose every match, including a 14-0 defeat by Myanmar. “Honestly, it was one of the worst teams in Syria’s history,” said Jumaa, who was part of that squad. “We lost by terrifying scores.”

Maha Al-Katreb, also in the squad at the time, remembers the criticism that followed. Players were ridiculed despite having had little preparation. At the tournament, she saw opponents arrive with larger coaching staffs and younger players training alongside their senior teams. The gap between Syria and their regional competitors was difficult to ignore.

With injuries ending her career early, Al-Katreb fell into coaching by chance and turned towards building a programme that could develop the next generation. She later joined the Syrian Football Association (SFA), taking on administrative and coaching responsibilities.

A six-team women’s senior league was established in 2019, followed by the development of youth national teams. This year the country held an inaugural edition of its youth league. Al-Katreb developed Syria’s first women’s football strategy, submitted to Fifa, that set out a longer-term plan for expanding participation and creating a pathway into the national teams. “You have to start building from the bottom if you want to see results after these 10 years,” Al-Katreb said. “So that we don’t burn one generation after another.”

In 2022, women accounted for only 1,000 of Syria’s 25,000 registered footballers. The women’s football strategy, seen by the Guardian, aimed to increase female participation by 150% over four years, including through 33 school training centres across 11 provinces, with capacity for 1,650 girls by 2026.

The government has also outlined plans to rehabilitate the country’s sporting infrastructure. Rami Alsubea, an adviser at the Ministry of Sport and Youth, said in a statement that 48 sports facilities had been rehabilitated in 2025, with plans to rehabilitate about 150 more and build about 20 new ones by 2028. Restoring infrastructure is in part to meet hosting criteria set by Fifa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Al-Katreb left the federation more than a year ago. Jumaa is now part of a two-woman team leading its women’s football department, appointed after the arrival of the federation’s current president, Feras al-Teet. Several players have criticized the federation’s leadership and the pace of progress. The Guardian reached out to Al-Teet for comment. He declined.

Among the players who have been vocal about the shortcomings is 26-year-old Rona Aizouk, one of the most experienced members of the current generation. Named after Brazilian footballer Ronaldinho, she made history in 2023 when she became the first Syrian-born woman to sign a professional contract, joining Saudi side Najmat Jeddah. Her performances in Syria had attracted the club’s attention, but securing the move proved difficult. Visa refusals and paperwork complications delayed her arrival until two days before the season began. Her time in Saudi Arabia lasted only a few months, and she was unable to extend her stay.

“Honestly, I went there not wanting to come back,” said Aizouk. “There’s no comparison. Everything is better, the treatment, the training, the facilities. It’s just different.

“The most important thing is the players’ comfort. Here in Syria, we have to endure psychological pressure and torment. As a player, I have to fight the world just to achieve even a little bit of success.”

After returning to Damascus to complete her studies, Aizouk quickly received interest from multiple clubs in Jordan, where she now plays. For her, being in situ abroad is about more than personal progression. “I want to be a message that I, who came out of hard circumstances and out of a war, still managed to succeed.”

Aizouk’s exposure to regional excellence has shown her that Syria is still many years behind. At the forefront is financial restriction that has left the sport bare-boned. International sanctions and banking restrictions imposed on Syria left millions of dollars in development funding from Fifa inaccessible to the SFA, preventing it from fully benefiting from programmes such as Fifa Forward.

Although broad economic sanctions have since been lifted, an estimated $11.5m in funds remains inaccessible to the federation. Both the SFA and Fifa insist they are working to establish a mechanism through which the money can be transferred. For now, the support has been seen in training equipment.

The financial strain is felt directly by players as both the national team and regional league are operated by the SFA. Clubs frequently go months without paying wages, and when payments do arrive, players say they can fall short of the amounts agreed. International call-ups offer little relief: during national team duty, including training camps, players receive a daily allowance of $20, capped at $200 for the length of their stay, regardless of how long it is. Some say the costs of travelling and playing can exceed what they receive.

Several clubs have folded since the domestic league’s launch in 2019, citing financial difficulties and the continued disruption caused by the war and ongoing conflicts. Those that remain often struggle to provide even basic resources.

Al-Hilal, now renamed Qamishlo Sport, have become one of the country’s most successful women’s sides, currently reigning as senior and youth league champions. But their achievements have not translated into financial security, according to head coach, Daleel Khalid. “There’s an absence of adequate support from all sides and the parties responsible for Syrian women’s sports, whether in terms of training camps and preparation, or the capabilities and infrastructure needed to develop the game,” he said.

The club’s campaign at the 2026 WAFF Women’s Clubs Championship was a big test. The tournament brought together league champions from six regional competitions. Despite having only a short training camp at home, Al-Hilal reached the final against Saudi champions Al-Nassr. Abo Lateef and Mustafa were among those who represented them, and their performances offered a reminder that Syrian teams can compete with the region’s best, even when their opponents have considerably greater resources.

There was also individual recognition. Al-Hilal’s Mai Al-Jani was named the tournament’s best player after a series of standout performances, an achievement she was quick to share with those around her. “The award I won is a source of pride for me, for the club and for the players. I see it as a team award,” she said. “It belongs to the staff, the players, and every Syrian girl living through these difficult circumstances.”

Born in 2006 in a small village in Homs province, Al-Jani has emerged as one of Syria’s promising attacking talents. She won the league’s Golden Boot in the 2024-25 season and has continued to impress for both club and country. She was also named the best player at the 2023 WAFF under-17 championship, when Syria won their first international title in women’s football. Al-Katreb, who was an assistant coach, saw the victory as evidence of what the country could build with the right support.

The WAFF under-17 triumph was repeated at the 2026 edition with a completely different squad. “It was joy that everyone in the country needed,” said Jumaa. “We were completely outnumbered in technical and admin staff, with only nine of us managing everything. Other teams had double the number of staff, with gameplay technology we can’t get our hands on.”

For Abo Lateef, the greatest risk is allowing another generation of players to lose the chance to compete. The senior women’s national team, for instance, has not played in over two years, with no reason given to players. “We need competition, regardless of the level,” said Abo Lateef. “I’m afraid a day will come when I’m made to sit at home, as was the case with the ones before us. A friendly fixture is a good start. Anything.”

Aizouk’s message to those responsible for the future of the women’s game was more direct. “Save Syrian football,” she said. “Save the generations. Save us.”

#883. ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi

Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

“I’d get asked to go to a job or I’d even get booked for a job and they’d be like: ‘Oh, we want you to come to Germany for three days,’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to say: ‘I can’t do it, my priority is football.’ As fun and different as [modelling] is, it’s not my main job. Football was my priority and is my priority.

“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done modelling. Going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris fashion week with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level that I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened.”

Sowunmi takes the Nobu Pilates with teacher Marsha Lindsay class twice a month in the five-star hotel of the same name in central London. He is an imposing presence at 1.98m (6ft 6in) tall and grimaces through the session as his muscles are put to the test to keep him in shape for both his professions. It helps him to battle robust strikers and appear on social media as part of modelling campaigns. “Two days ago one of my current coaches said: ‘You popped up wearing a coat on my Instagram the other day. Can you get me one?’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to explain that it doesn’t really work like that.”

Sowunmi’s career path since he left his first club, Ipswich, without making an appearance has been that of a true lower-league player, taking in spells at Yeovil, Colchester and – between two stints with Bromley – Sutton. On the catwalk, he has rubbed shoulders with some of the biggest names in the industry while promoting designer brands and plans to continue doing that once he retires from the day job. He uses social media not only to post videos and images from photoshoots but to show the reality of life as a footballer.

“The fans and everyone that watches you on Saturday or Tuesday or whatever day you’re playing, they get to see you for 90 minutes and they don’t see the full dedication that goes into being a professional footballer,” Sowunmi says. “We’re away from our families for two days [for away games]; we’ll train on the Friday then leave, maybe have a seven-hour coach journey. We’ll have stuff to do at the hotel, stretching sessions, pool sessions, nutrition. We’ll wake up and we’ll have more stuff to do and it’s that whole buildup that I kind of want to show them and give them an insight into what we do.”

Last season Sowunmi helped Bromley gain promotion to third tier for the first time. The step up has been difficult, costing the long-serving manager Andy Woodman his job. “It’s been tough, as you can tell by the league position,” Sowunmi says. “It’s a completely different league. It’s taken a lot of the players by surprise, the difference between League One and League Two, but we’re grinding, we’re working hard and I’m sure it will turn for us.”

A carefully curated moustache sits atop Sowunmi’s lip to raise money for Movember. He is speaking at a charity event on Wednesday to highlight the importance of mental health, a subject close to his heart since his best friend took his own life. “It’s something that is really deep in my heart just being a voice for people and trying to help make a difference in any way that I can,” Sowunmi says. “I was actually on an away trip and I received a call from his dad to give me the news.

“Everyone was asking me what was wrong on the bus and that I wasn’t really speaking to anyone and then I think when we got home it was a four-, five-hour journey. The manager took me to the side and got me to open up to him a little bit. Looking back that actually helped a lot, so I thought if I can help someone to speak to someone or know that it’s fine to speak to someone then I’m definitely here for it.”

#881. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

#880. Retraction Note: Detection of anisotropic cosmic structures on a gigaparsec scale

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026

Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026

The authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Our calculations were erroneously comparing the comoving distance between the observed galaxies to the luminosity distance between galaxies in the simulated mocks. Correcting these issues reduces the discrepancy between the observed and simulated samples to 1.48–2.75 sigma, depending on the sample construction. This falls below the standard significance threshold of 3 sigma in the cosmology literature.

Despite the revised uncertainties, our method remains valid and provides tentative evidence for anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Universe. The revised paper, with corrected uncertainties, will be submitted to another journal. This retraction will contain a link to the new publication, if and when it is published.

Sawala, T. The local galaxy distribution does not violate the cosmological principle. Astrophys. J. Lett. 1007, L22 https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ae908f (2026).

#879. Summer signings join Lionel Messi among MLS’s top earners: Takeaways from the league’s salary release

How much in player salaries did it take to earn a point in the 2026 MLS regular season? The latest batch of salaries lends some insight

Lionel Messi has closer company at the top of MLS’s list of highest-paid players, thanks to another pair of former Barcelona attackers. The Inter Miami captain is still comfortably the league’s top earner, on a guaranteed compensation of $28.3m. Robert Lewandowski (Chicago Fire) and Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City) have entered the list with the second and third highest wages, while Atlanta United’s Breel Embolo, another summer signing, ranks fifth on a guaranteed compensation of $10.8m. Second-year LAFC forward Son Heung-min sits fourth on $11.2m.

Casimiro, who joined Messi in Miami at the end of his contract with Manchester United, is his team’s fourth top-earner with a guaranteed compensation of $3.54m. This comes after Miami announced his signing as a non-designated player to the surprise of some as the Brazilian arrived on a Bosman transfer rather than a loan-with-purchase, as Rodrigo De Paul had last summer, to keep Miami rules compliant. The MLS Players’ Association lists Casimiro on a base salary of $896,004.

All of these earnings figures were revealed as part of the MLS Players’ Association’s twice-a-year data dump, with the latter installment dropping hours before the league’s postseason commenced. While these figures don’t include transfer fees and therefore don’t tell the whole picture of a team’s investment in its roster, it’s a useful bit of insight in regards to how each team is spending on player wages.

Figures are players’ guaranteed compensation inclusive of base salary and all guaranteed bonuses; does not include marketing and other bonuses.

Thirteen of MLS’s 30 clubs have a new highest earner after a busy post-World Cup transfer window. Two – Anders Dreyer (San Diego, $3.6m) and Mateusz Bogusz (Houston, $2.5m) – rose to the top after the departure of a higher-paid teammate. Lozano overtook the injured Riqui Puig after arriving with the LA Galaxy on loan from San Diego. Lewandowski, Griezmann, and Embolo hold similar status, while Charlotte replaced Wilfried Zaha with Allan Saint-Maximin ($7.2m) earning nearly three times as much as the Crystal Palace great.

Other top-earners signed from beyond the league are Brais Méndez (Columbus, $5.2m), André Luiz (Kansas City, $3.3m), and Kai Wagner (Philadelphia, $1.6m). Two strikers who were traded within the league mid-season signed fresh terms that made them their new teams’ highest-paid players: Rafael Navarro (St. Louis, $4.95m) and Dejan Joveljic (Seattle, $3.7m).

The standout failure of the new big earners is Alexis Sánchez. The 37-year-old Chile legend came to North America this summer, joining CF Montréal and making 15 league appearances for the Quebecois club but failing to register a single goal or assist. His $2.97m guaranteed compensation makes up 24.6% of the team’s wage bill.

Griezmann’s arrival means that Messi no longer carries the largest share of any team’s wage bill, as Orlando has dedicated slightly more to the Frenchman (49.5%) than Miami has to the Argentinian (47.7%). Lewandowski narrowly trails by accounting for 47.3% of Chicago’s wage spending. Importantly, Messi’s contract includes add-ons; a portion of Apple TV subscriptions, merchandise sales through Adidas and Fanatics, and an optional ownership stake in Miami when he retires.

Other notable new wages include former Middlesbrough attacking midfielder Morgan Whittaker (Colorado, $2.0m), former Watford and Everton midfielder Abdoulaye Doucouré (Charlotte, $1.0m), former Manchester United left-back Tyrell Malacia (Cincinnati, $1.04m), former NYCFC playmaker Santi Rodríguez (Columbus, $3.9m), South Africa striker Lyle Foster (Houston, $1.8m), former Celtic striker Kyōgo Furuhashi (LA Galaxy, $1.1m), Tunisia winger Elias Saad (Nashville, $1.7m), former Leeds winger Jack Harrison (New England, $3.65m), Côte d’Ivoire winger Bénie Traoré (NYCFC, $2.5m), former Netherlands striker Vincent Janssen (Portland, $1.75m), Tunisia winger Elias Achouri (San Diego, $2.6m), Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn (San Jose, $1.6m), and Southampton loanee Damion Downs (St Louis, $1.6m).

While this exercise cannot confidently include every transfer fee paid, the timing of this year’s drop after the regular season’s end allows us to size up how teams spent on wages against the league table.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Does spending more equal success? There’s a degree of correlation there, but it’s not strong.

How valuable is it to get a point in MLS? In 2026’s wage economy, exactly $512,394.

So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Top 10 European Strikers of the Century - Part One

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."

Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.

The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."

Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."

Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."

Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."

Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."

The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.

Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."

Balague: "What could have been, yes. He was the national team's record scorer too before Harry Kane took it. I find him to deserve this place as he had to adapt to a lot of strikers and he did it well. He had the ability to link up and score. He was very intelligent."

Laurens: "He is the most street footballer England has ever seen. There's no rules, that kind of anger you saw on the pitch. I don't think people in England realise how good he was."

What does becoming the all-time World Cup top goalscorer get you? Sixth place on the best European strikers this century list. The Real Madrid forward, 27, just misses out on the top five.

Laurens: "Maybe if we do this ranking again in a few years he will be higher. I would have had him top five, for sure. He has scored more than 400 goals. I don't think Messi and Ronaldo had scored that many at that age, so he's ahead. I don't know if he will play for as long as them but he hasn't done much wrong in his career."

Balague: "This list has to do what you feel about the player, not science - 22 goals in 22 appearances in World Cups and [Euro] Championships. He should be at least top three because of that. Great stats, but we're not in love with him."

Honigstein: "I don't think there is a forward that is as good as footballer as him in 2026. On that basis alone he should be higher, but people when they vote have other things in their head. The only way to win everyone over is to score more goals and win more World Cups for France, which I think is possible."

There was little between Mbappe and Erling Haaland, but it is Manchester City's prolific Norwegian who slips in at fifth. The 26-year-old has already scored more than 300 club goals and has a staggering 68 in 61 games for his country.

Balague: "Mbappe should be higher than him. Haaland scored 52 goals in 53 games [in 2022-23], that is astonishing, but he's gone 11 finals without scoring. We're talking about the best. We're talking about what we see at the moment and what we see is someone who is calculated but in a more charming way. An ability to score we haven't seen in a while; power, ability to finish. He is not world class to the level of others."

Honigstein: "I don't think it's fair to judge him on just that. They [Manchester City] won the Champions League when he was there. When Haaland arrived with Pep Guardiola, they found a way to do it. What makes him unique is the physical attributes and the pace. To have both is unique. He can sprint like a 100m sprinter. Is he the fifth best striker of the 21st Century? I don't think he's that far behind."

Interesting, this, because Robert Lewandowski is well clear of Haaland in fourth, but the leap from the Polish forward to the top three is massive - more than 10,000 votes.

The 38-year-old is still chipping away for Chicago Fire in Major League Soccer, having been a reliably ruthless assassin for Barcelona, Bayern and Dortmund.

Honigstein: "He used to play basketball, judo, handball - his father wanted him to have a wholesome education. You could see his completeness that he had as a centre-forward. Nothing in his game was extraordinary but in terms of ticking all the boxes, none come close to him."

Balague: "He said he learned to be an elite striker when he forgot what he had just done, like a fish. Mistakes he had in his head affected his performance. One day he just continued like it didn't matter."

Laurens: "He won the Ballon d'Or in Covid, it won't be on his mantlepiece but we all know it was his."

Fresh from his Ballon d'Or triumph, England's record goalscorer and appearance maker rides into the top three on the back of 61 goals in 51 outings for Bayern Munich last season.

Kane left the Premier League three years ago with the second-most goals ever in the competition, and is also Tottenham's all-time record scorer.

Honigstein: "Third place, at least. He is doing incredible things. At 33, still not quite at his peak. I don't think he relies on his pace, physicality, it's all about intelligence, technique. I don't think there's anyone in the game that strikes a ball as well as him right now. I don't think any player comes close that we've talked about so far in overall work-rate, defending, helping the team, making tackles in your box in the 90th minute when you're 3-0 up because he's that kind of guy. He is humble and a superb human being."

Laurens: "What I love about Kane, from a young age, a lot of this list you just knew the trajectory would be all the way to the top. Kane was not like that. It could have been very different for him. Nobody at 17 would've said he was going to win the Ballon d'Or. Nobody believed in him like the others. Kane had a very different journey."

Runner-up Thierry Henry is the only striker in the top six who is retired. A World Cup and Euros winner with France, Henry won titles with Arsenal - where he scored 228 goals - and a Champions League with Barcelona.

Honigstein: "During his time, I don't think there was a player like him in the Premier League. The way he played football was stylish, elegant, but there was almost a kind of a romantic connection between him and the ball. I don't think there was anyone near that kind of level of technique and, for want of a better word, va-va-voom he exuded. That just made for amazing viewing."

Laurens: "For me as a fellow Parisien, he's a very special player, a very special man. A career that has been incredible from a young age. It's that season in the Premier League - 24 goals, 20 assists in 38 games - not even Kane or Benzema or Cristiano, OK, Messi is different, but they haven't done that and yet he did it.

"There are still some people who undervalue him and underappreciate him and the monster that he was on the football pitch. He had it all. The pace, the style, the elegance, the technique, the mentality, the goals, the aura, the charisma. Just everything you wanted if you were to build a striker. One of the greatest football brains ever."

Of course, at number one, it's the man chasing the 1,000-goal dream. Cristiano Ronaldo may have retired from Portugal duty with 146 notches on his strike chart but the quest goes on at Al-Nassr.

The 41-year-old's evolution from tricky winger to prolific frontman has taken him from Sporting to Manchester United, twice, Real Madrid, Juventus and now Saudi Arabia.

Balague: "He's the best striker in history. His numbers are incredible. He won't stop until he gets to 1,000. He is somebody who is special. We know his background, how he wanted to be Ballon d'Or winner at 12 and didn't stop until he got there. He ran up the mountains of Funchal with weights in his ankles and snuck into the gym when it was closed to get the physique he wanted."

Laurens: "Always in the right place at the right time. The instinct. He was born with a gift, like all in this list. But you still have to work hard. Nobody will ever reach those levels again. 1,000 goals for club and country will never be done again, I think."

Honigstein: "Peak Ronaldo for me was Gareth Bale scoring and him looking very unhappy. I don't think there will be any dispute about him being the greatest. Somebody who has done it all, won it all, and he's still going for the love of it."

#876. What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season

Past years suggest it is tough to make big positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated

The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged.

Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing.

There have inevitably been outliers. Tottenham have tumbled by at least 10 places after matchweek 10 in the past two seasons and Newcastle (in 2021-22), Crystal Palace and Everton (both 2017-18) have risen from the relegation zone at this point to the safety of mid-table by May.

But even moving one position across the remainder of the season can make an enormous difference to a team on the fringe of the Champions League qualification spots, or to those that sit 17th or 18th after 10 games. Not since 2006-07 have the bottom three clubs with 28 matches to go all been relegated.

This fact feels especially relevant this season given two of the three teams in the drop zone have changed their manager since the previous round of matches. Sunderland have stood by Régis Le Bris but he is the favourite to be the next Premier League manager to leave their post. If we can reasonably assume at least one of the clubs currently 18th to 20th will be in the top flight in 2027-28, which is best placed to survive?

It is going to be very tough for Crystal Palace. Opta’s underlying data model implies they are where they deserve to be in the table, whereas Manchester United and Sunderland should be much higher. The largest improvement Palace’s new manager, Thomas Frank, engineered between weeks 10 and 38 at Brentford was two places, which will not cut it this season. Palace have to take inspiration from the 2024-25 season, in which they also had seven points after 10 games yet rose to finish 12th.

Mauricio Pochettino’s Chelsea were 11th going into their 11th game in 2023-24 before ending sixth. As they were also 11th in early April, they made a much shorter dash to the finish line, though. Pochettino’s teams usually improve as campaigns wear on, with Tottenham rising three places after week 10 in each of his first three seasons with the club. A similar lift in his new role would not make this season a rousing success for United but it would stave off the unthinkable idea of relegation.

For someone to escape, someone else must take their place. Ignoring the possibility that the answer to “who?” may be Manchester City, the team in 17th are inevitably the ones most at risk. Of the 13 sides in the past decade who were outside the drop zone after 10 games but went down, six were fourth-bottom going into matchweek 11.

Given that the points gap between first and 20th (20) was last lower at this stage in 2015-16, those figures may be more pertinent than position this season. Leeds in 2022-23 and Bournemouth three years earlier had 13 points after 10 games but were relegated, as did Blackpool in 2010-11 and Middlesbrough two seasons before them.

Only nine clubs are now above that bar, with Aston Villa, Newcastle and Tottenham among those who are not. The table is unlikely to change too much before the end of the campaign but there is a distinct chance that a secure-looking side will perish.
